messages.subject: Reparametrization and PC-prior in latent model
messages.subject_clean: Reparametrization and PC-prior in latent model
messages.body_plain:
Dear R-inla list

I have data which can be modelled as follows:

n = 100
prec.1=1
prec.2=5
nb = 4
nz1 = 5
nz2 = 10
Z1 = kronecker(diag(nz1),rep(1,20))
Z2 = matrix(runif(n*nz2), n, nz2)
b1 = rnorm(nz1,mean=0,sd=1/sqrt(prec.1))
b2 = rnorm(nz2,mean=0,sd=1/sqrt(prec.2))
beta = 5 + rnorm(nb)
X = matrix(runif(n*nb), n, nb)
X[,1] = 1
eta = X %*% beta + Z1 %*% b1 + Z2 %*% b2
y = eta + rnorm(n, sd=0.01)

formula = y ~ -1 + X + f(id.z1, model="z", Z=Z1)+f(id.z2, model="z", Z=Z2)
result = inla(formula, data = list(y=y, id.z1 = 1:n,id.z2 = 1:n, X=X))

So it is a model with 2 random effects: one which is a sort of clustering random effect and another which is a more global random effect (for example a spatial effect although there is nothing spatial in the example above)
I am interested in a base model (or standard model) which is the model with only the cluster random effects, that is eta = X %*% beta + Z1 %*% b1. The model with two random effects is a generalization of the base model which I would like to use only if the base model does not fit well.

My question is if it is possible to fit my model in similar way as can be done with the  "bym2" model described in

http://inla.googlecode.com/hg-history/475192f4b6f3668d2637e54547517b3747082e16/r-inla.org/doc/latent/bym2.pdf

So basically v* would correspond to  Z1 %*% b1 and u* would correspond to  Z2 %*% b2.

If this is possible my other question is  if it is then possible to use this in combination with  the PC-priors of Simpson et al (2014)  more or less in the same way is done in the code shown in

http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/case-studies/Martins-etal-2014/bym/bym.R

Thanks in advance

Karim

messages.subject: Correlated Random coefficient logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
Simmons and Higgins have recently described a Correlated random coefficient logistic regression for diagnostic meta analysis:,
Logit(P_ik) = mu_i +  theta_i*A_ik
Where P_ik is the probability of positive test result in group k of study i and A_ik indicates whether the group has the medical condition according to the gold standard test (k=1: affected; k=0:not affected) with A=0 or A=1

mu_i and theta_i  have random effects which are bivariate normally distributed with means mu and theta; variances tausq_mu and tausq_theta and correlation rho.
How may I code this using R-INLA?
Reference: DOI: 10.1177/0962280214534409
Simmonds and Higgins SMMR 2014

messages.subject: Defining a inla.mesh.2d for a body of water
messages.subject_clean: Defining a inla.mesh.2d for a body of water
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've been setting up an INLA model to make some inferences on spatio-temporal tendencies of count data observed at different sites near the coast line in bays/inlets etc.

These counts are not observable on land so I need to specify a boundary for inla.mesh.2d so that my spatial random field only considers the body of water.

Is there an easy way to do this with mapdata (ie worldHires)?

I have polygons of land masses but am finding it hard to do this with bodies of water and each attempt with inla.nonconvex.hull() has produced really jagged meshes with far too many nodes at the boundary.

Another option could be to have multiple inner domains in my mesh separated by land (then I don't think having the outer domain overlap land would matter so much).

Is this possible with inla.mesh.2d?

Any advice or help would be greatly appreciated, thanks!

Hayden

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Correlated Random coefficient logistic regression
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: Correlated Random coefficient logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
That's straightforward. Combining the FAQ and copy example, you get this:

n=1000
i=1:n
j = i
z = rnorm(n)
w = runif(n)
y = z  + 2*z*w + rnorm(n)
t = as.numeric(y>0) # threshold model, equivalent to a probit link.
But it looks looks a logit
formula = y ~ f(i, model="iid",initial=0, fixed=T) +
  f(j, w, copy="i", fixed=FALSE)
r = inla(formula, data = data.frame(i,j,w,y))

formula = t ~ f(i, model="iid",initial=0, fixed=T) +
  f(j, w, copy="i", fixed=FALSE)
r = inla(formula, data = data.frame(i,j,w,y,t),  family = "binomial",
Ntrials = rep(1, n),
         control.family = list(link = "logit"))

Which should be easy to apply to your situation.

Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 2015-02-16 at 23:08 -0800, Anand Patil wrote:
> Hi everyone,
>
>
> Is it feasible to estimate ahead of time roughly how much memory
> inla(...) will use? As a fallback, is it feasible to estimate the
> dependence of memory usage on the num.threads argument?

not possible...

In general the memory use is

	A + B * number.of.threads

for some positive number A and B..

control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian")

is a simpler approximation and will also reduce the memory use. adding
int.strategy="eb" is another one, and combined, gives you a lower
bound.

Best

messages.subject_clean: Change the prior of the fixed effects?
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I would like to use a Laplace prior (aka double-exponential) for two of the  fixed effects (not the intercept) in a Poisson regression model. Is it possible to do  something like this in INLA? This is because the model where those two fixed effects are zero corresponds to base model I am interested in.  The model where those fixed effects are nonzero is a generalization of the base model and (if I understand correctly) these Laplace priors follow the principles of PC prior specification of Simpson et al 2014 . Also, I understand these priors are used commonly in the variable selection context so it would useful for this other reason

Thanks in advance
Karim

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Change the prior of the fixed effects?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karim,
I'm on my phone, travelling, so I can only be brief.

The posterior for the Laplace prior (the Bayesian lasso) does not have good variable selection properties. The horseshoe (putting a half Cauchy on the standard deviation [not variance!] of the normal) is far far better.

For the PC prior framework, we would recommend an exponential prior instead of w half Cauchy. This works fine with low dimensions, but as the number of covariates increase, the heavy tail of the half Cauchy makes a difference (for the better).

That said, you can do it if you want. It would be

f(index, covariate, model="iid", hyper=list(prec=list(........)))

Where the hyper specification puts the appropriate prior on the precision that makes this marginally a Laplace distribution.

Hope this helps,

Dan

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Dan for the quick and illuminative reply! Just to confirm and for full info to all those interested

In the command

f(index, covariate, model="iid", hyper=list(prec=list(........)))

you mean index is  the vector of ones, covariate is the vector of weights with the covariate values
and the hyper prior specification is that of an exponential distribution for the variance (not the std dev) which leads to a Laplace marginal for the "random effect" called  here index. Also to see the corresponding posterior we would need to check in model$marginals.random instead of using model$marginals.fixed. Also, this trick will work only if we know a mixture of normals representation of the distribution we want for index.

Please correct me if I am wrong!

Karim

messages.subject: Double hierarchical GLMs in INLA?
messages.body_plain:
Is is possible to construct double hierarchical GLMMs in INLA, i.e. model the (log-)variance as well as the mean? (ref: Lee, Y. and Nelder, J. A. (2006). Double hierarchical generalized linear models (with discussion),Applied Statistics 55, 139–185).

This is a toy example:
N <- 100
X <- 1:N
E.Y <- 5 + 0.4*X
Var.Y <- exp(5-0.1*X)
Y <- rnorm(N, E.Y, sqrt(Var.Y))

plot(X,E.Y, type="l", ylab="y")
points(X,Y)

For my problem I need random effects in both the mean and variance parts of the model, but at least it's Gaussian.
